Governing body: International Association of Information Technology Asset Managers (IAITAM)
Typical domains: Cross-industry; any sector emphasis is unverified
Pros: Foundational, broad process view; assumes no specialization
Cons: Doesn't go deep on software or hardware specifics; annual renewal

Governing body: International Association of Information Technology Asset Managers (IAITAM)
Typical domains: Large software estates facing vendor true-up risk: finance, healthcare, government, any enterprise running Microsoft/Oracle/SAP-scale license agreements
Pros: Ties directly to three of this kit's tools (`rationalization`, `itam-maturity`, `audit-response`); most audit-relevant of the three IAITAM credentials listed here

Governing body: International Association of Information Technology Asset Managers (IAITAM)
Typical domains: Hardware-fleet-heavy sectors: manufacturing, healthcare (medical equipment), education (device fleets), retail/logistics (warehouse and POS hardware), government
Pros: The only one of the six covering physical assets; ties directly to this kit's `hardware-lifecycle` tool

Typical domains: Deliberately cross-industry by design: any sector deploying AI, in compliance/legal/risk/data-science roles rather than a particular vertical
Pros: The only AI-focused credential here; industry-agnostic; ties to `ai-intake`
Cons: Separate body/ecosystem from the IAITAM three; harder exam format (multi-select, no partial credit); one recertification detail is flagged below as unconfirmed

Best for: Anyone working in or around IT service delivery
Typical domains: Complex, service-heavy IT environments: banking, insurance, healthcare, telecommunications, government, and managed-service/IT-outsourcing providers
Cons: Not asset-management-specific; its ties to this kit's tools are real but indirect; renewal every 3 years

Best for: People new to (or early in) formal asset management, beyond IT alone
Typical domains: Asset-intensive, infrastructure-heavy sectors: utilities (water, electricity, gas), transport and rail, oil and gas, mining, manufacturing, airports, government and public infrastructure
Pros: Built on general asset management beyond IT; its syllabus follows the logic of the ISO 55000 series, which traces back to PAS 55, a specification the IAM helped develop
Cons: UK-centered exam logistics (Pearson-approved IAM venues); no IT- or software-specific content of its own
